title: Unique ID generation
subtitle: Every row, request and event needs a name that no other has. Learn the main ways to create IDs, and what each one costs your database, your clocks and your security.

c.v: This story is made up, but each part of it is common.
A shop app keeps orders in one PostgreSQL table. The

Both bugs come from the same choice: an ID that was only unique inside one database, and easy to guess.
An ID names one thing, forever. You use IDs as

A good ID scheme answers four questions. Can many machines create IDs without asking each other? Do IDs sort by time? How big are they? Can outsiders guess them?
Pick the ID scheme for the scale you will have, not the scale you have today. Changing it later means changing every table, API and URL that holds an ID.

Any machine can make one, with no coordination.
Random keys have a cost in a
9562 says UUID v4 has "poor database-index locality".
Each new key lands on a random page. InnoDB reports that keys inserted in order leave index pages about 15/16 full. Keys inserted in random order leave them between 1/2 and 15/16 full.

UUID v7 keeps the UUID format but puts time first. The first 48 bits are the Unix time in milliseconds. Then come the version, 12 random bits, the variant, and 62 more random bits. A generator may put a counter in some of the random bits, to keep order within one millisecond.
So new IDs sort after older ones, and new values sit near each other in the index. The RFC says this gives better database-index locality. It says the difference from random inserts "can be one
It also says implementations should use v7 instead of the older time-based versions, v1 and v6, if possible.

In 2010, Twitter was replacing many MySQL systems with Cassandra or sharded MySQL. Neither had a built-in way to create unique IDs. Twitter needed tens of thousands of IDs per second, from a highly available service. So it chose an approach with no coordination.
Each ID has three parts: a timestamp, a worker number and a sequence number.

The README gives the sizes. The time takes 41 bits, in milliseconds from a custom epoch, which lasts 69 years. The machine ID takes 10 bits, for up to 1,024 machines. The sequence takes 12 bits, so it rolls over every 4,096 IDs per machine.
That is 63 bits, so the ID fits in a signed 64-bit integer. Worker numbers were chosen at startup through ZooKeeper, or set in a config file.
Step through how one ID is built.
IDs from one machine sort by time, because time sits in the top bits. Across machines, the order is only rough. Twitter called its IDs "roughly sortable".
The README says they are "k-sorted" within a bound: it promised 1 second and aimed for tens of milliseconds.

is 128 bits, like a UUID: a 48-bit millisecond timestamp, then 80 random bits. It is written as 26 characters, not the 36 of a UUID, and the text sorts in time order. The spec says it allows 1.21e+24 unique IDs per millisecond. Within one millisecond, order is not guaranteed. An optional monotonic mode adds one to the random part instead. If that overflows, generation fails.
In our view, UUID v7 now gives you most of the same benefits in the standard UUID format.

Do not hand out guessable IDs
Sequential IDs in URLs invite people to try the next number. OWASP's example of this bug uses a "fairly predictable, perhaps sequential" ID. It is a form of
Random IDs make guessing harder, but OWASP says that is "generally not sufficient by itself".
The fix is an access check on every request. See
. RFC 9562 also warns: do not assume UUIDs are hard to guess, and never use one as a secret that grants access.

For UUID v4, think of 122 random bits. That is about 5.3 × 10^36 possible values. By our own arithmetic, with the standard birthday estimate, you would need about 2.3 × 10^18 IDs before the chance of even one clash reaches about 40%. RFC 9562 itself gives no numbers. It says true global uniqueness cannot be guaranteed without shared knowledge. It asks you to weigh what a clash would cost your application.
Our view: in practice, a clash is far more likely to come from a bug, like a copied seed or a reused machine number, than from bad luck.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: "Will this table ever live on more than one database?"
If yes, do not depend on auto-increment.
Separate the internal key from the public ID if you must. A table can keep a small integer key and also store a random public ID for URLs.
Never let an ID replace an
check. Test that user A cannot read user B's object by changing the ID.
, write down how machine IDs are assigned and freed. Two generators with the same machine ID can create the same IDs.
Alert when an ID generator refuses to work because of the clock. It means NTP or the host has a problem.
Use 64-bit integer columns, or the database's UUID type. Do not store UUIDs as long strings without a reason.
Never promise gapless IDs from a sequence. If finance needs gapless numbers, design that separately.
"List every table in this schema with its primary key type. For each one, say whether it would still be unique if we split the table across two databases."
"Find every API route that takes an ID from the URL or body. For each, show where the code checks that the caller may access that object. Flag any route without such a check."

"Write a test for our ID generator. Make 1 million IDs on 8 threads, check that none repeat, and check that IDs from one thread always go up. Then move the fake clock back by 5 ms and show what happens."
The UUID version the agent's code produces is the one you want. Check the library docs, and do not assume.
Any bit layout adds up to 64 or fewer bits, and the time part lasts long enough from your chosen epoch.
The agent did not treat random IDs as security. Every object access still has an owner check.

q.v: You split an orders table over two MySQL shards. Both still use AUTO_INCREMENT with default settings. What happens?

options.v: Nothing. MySQL makes IDs unique across servers.
Both shards start at 1, so two different orders get the same ID.
MySQL refuses to insert on the second shard.

why.v: Each server counts on its own. You must give them different offsets, or generate IDs outside the databases.

q.v: Why can random UUID v4 primary keys slow down inserts into a large B-tree index?

options.v: Each new key lands on a random page, so the index loses locality and pages end up less full.
UUIDs cannot be stored in a B-tree.
Random keys force the database to rebuild the index after each insert.

why.v: RFC 9562 says UUID v4 has poor database-index locality. InnoDB says random inserts leave pages 1/2 to 15/16 full.

q.v: In a Snowflake-style ID, why do IDs from one machine sort by time?

options.v: Because the machine number is in the top bits.
Because the timestamp is in the top bits, so a later millisecond always gives a bigger number.
Because a central server hands them out in order.

why.v: The time sits above the machine and the sequence bits. Any later millisecond beats any value in the lower bits.

q.v: Your order page URL is /orders/10452, using an auto-increment ID. What is the main risk?

options.v: Someone can try 10451, 10453 and so on. If the server does not check ownership, they see other people's orders.
The browser cannot cache the page.

why.v: Sequential IDs are easy to guess. The real fix is an authorization check on every request. Random IDs only make guessing harder.

q.v: A Snowflake-style generator sees that the clock moved back by 2 ms. What should it do?

options.v: Keep going with the new time.
Refuse to create IDs until the clock passes the last time it used.

why.v: An older time could repeat earlier IDs or break the order. Twitter's Snowflake refuses until the time is after the last one it used.
